newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal can enter EMU if it wants to - Chirac.
newsitem.headline: Portugal can enter EMU if it wants to - Chirac.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac gave a verbal boost on Monday to Portugal's hopes of being a founder of a single European currency, saying Portugal would be able to take part if it wants to.

"I don't want to interfere in the internal affairs of Portugal, but my conviction is that if it wants to, it can without doubt (enter EMU at the agreed-upon date)," Chirac told reporters after a lunch with Portuguese Prime Minister Antonio Guterres.
When asked under what conditions Portugal could join the single currency, Chirac said it would have to adhere to the terms of the Maastricht treaty.

"Exclusively by the letter of the treaty. All the signatories of the Maastricht treaty have the same right, exactly the same right, to enter EMU from the start on the condition naturally that they satisfy the necessary convergence criteria," Chirac said.
European Union countries are racing to cut deficits and public debt to levels demanded by the Maastricht treaty in order to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU).

Chirac's statements, combined with comments by Guterres in a French newspaper on Monday, made clear Portugal's determination to stand out from other southern European nations that are having more trouble meeting the Maastricht-treaty targets.
In financial daily Les Echos, Guterres said any country meeting criteria for a single currency should be allowed in to EMU.
He said it would be a violation of the Maastricht treaty to exclude Portugal from the launch of a single currency simply because it is a southern European country.
Guterres's comments were similar to those by leaders of the other countries concerned, Italy and Spain, who have said hard economic data should determine EMU membership.
Guterres expressed confidence that Portugal would be able to meet criteria for the single currency on time.
"What gives me confidence is that the Portuguese economy is healthy," Guterres said.

"Its growth is higher than the European average, its unemployment is lower. That proves that our convergence efforts are sustainable: the public deficit, inflation, interest rates and the foreign exchange rate show the escudo will bring a positive contribution to the euro," he said.

Spain, which has pledged to do what is needed to become a founding member of EMU, and Portugal both appear to stand a better chance of meeting strict Maastricht-treaty criteria for EMU, but the idea of allowing them to join while excluding EU founder Italy may be politically difficult.

Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi has staked his political future to first wave membership of EMU, inflicting budgetary rigour on Italy and the prospect of more austerity in the run-up to a decision in early 1998 on which countries can join.
